practice.title: Reconnaissance on Your Mind
agreedSteps: Do surveillance on your mental terrain: each day, write down what's annoying you, what you're craving, what you're resisting. Be honest and specific — this is discovery, not judgment.
Look for easy wins. Don't dismiss the small, petty delusions that flicker through the day. Minor non-acceptances and little craving moments are actually rich territory for growth.
steps: Make mental action your first resort, not your last. When a difficulty arises, try to transform it from the inside before reaching for an external fix.

Once you've identified your terrain, pick the right Dharma tool for the specific delusion you're working with — it might be bodhichitta, great compassion, wishing love, equanimity, or exchanging self with others. There are no wrong answers.
Don't think anything is too small or trivial to work on. What would it be like to have no minor non-acceptance in the week ahead? That would actually be a blissful week.
practice.quote: What would it be like to have no minor non-acceptance in the week ahead? Fantastic day. We'd be blissful actually I think if we completely unraveled all of our little minor non-acceptances.

commentary.title: The Power of Mental Actions
content: The entire benefits-of-bodhichitta section of Meaningful to Behold is making one point, over and over: mental actions are unbelievably potent. We believe in the power of physical actions to some degree, but the Buddhist understanding is that mental actions are millions of times more powerful. One beneficial intention — directed merely at relieving the suffering of others' headaches — can purify a lifetime of heavy negative karma and instantly end a hellish rebirth. What does that mean for all of our mental actions throughout the day?

The whole world right now is pouring extraordinary wealth and ingenuity into data centers the size of cities just to try to create a mind. And each of us has one of those already — and more than what they can create — in our clear light mind, in the root mind at our heart. Our mind is a world-builder. It can turn an enemy into a kind mother. Nothing else out there can do that — not diplomacy, not technology. But the mind can. The mind can turn poison into nectar. The mind can turn us into a Buddha.
commentary.quote: My mind is like a world builder. My mind is a realm builder. It can create a realm. Basically an entire reality with a thought.

commentary.title: Aspiring and Engaging Bodhichitta
content: The aspiring mind of bodhichitta is the wish to attain enlightenment for the benefit of all beings. The engaging mind is when we actually take the Bodhisattva vows and engage in the practices — the six perfections — that lead there. Both are extraordinary, but there is an important distinction: the aspiring mind is like wishing to make a journey, while the engaging mind is like actually setting out. From the moment the Bodhisattva vows are fully taken, merit arises without interruption — even when the Bodhisattva is asleep, unconcerned, or apparently intoxicated.

Whatever actions of body, speech and mind a person with the engaging mind undertakes become a cause for the attainment of the highest enlightenment. This is the difference between ordinary virtue — however sincere — and the virtue of a Bodhisattva whose every action is saturated with the intention to liberate all beings.

commentary.title: Buddha Shakyamuni's Previous Life
content: The story of Buddha Shakyamuni's previous life is a perfect illustration of the power of a single beneficial intention. In that life, he created heavy negative karma by fighting with his mother and was reborn in a hell realm, where his head was continually bored into. Around him were other beings experiencing the same torment. When the sight of their suffering stirred a compassionate wish in his heart — 'How wonderful it would be if all sentient beings were separated from these pains; may all such suffering ripen upon me' — the entire karmic debt from harming his mother was completely purified in that instant. He was immediately reborn in a pure realm.

This is taking and giving in its purest form. And it illustrates something worth really sitting with: a single beneficial intention, arising from the heart in response to the suffering of others, can undo lifetimes of negative karma. That power is available to each of us.

commentary.title: Merit: Real Good Fortune
content: When Geshe-la finally gave a clear definition of merit — in the Mirror of Dharma teachings — he said it means 'real good fortune,' which technically means the cause of spiritual realizations. Not a good job, not high position, not favorable external circumstances. Those things are not merit. Whether external good fortune is even beneficial depends entirely on whether it leads to spiritual realizations. Without that, it could actually be a kind of curse — a distraction from what really matters.

This is another reason mental actions are so powerful: they are precisely what creates merit. A beneficial intention directed toward one hundred beings creates one hundred merits. Toward a thousand beings, a thousand merits. Toward countless beings — as in bodhichitta — the merits are limitless. The Bodhisattva's motivation is the most potent merit-creating force in existence.

commentary.title: Diagnosing a Meditation That Isn't Working
content: When a Lamrim meditation just doesn't groove — doesn't spark anything, doesn't produce the feeling it's supposed to — there's usually a hidden obstacle rather than no obstacle at all. Three diagnostic tools are worth exploring. First: get the right object. Sometimes our conception of the meditation's object is diametrically opposed to its actual nature. We may have mapped an unpleasant personal experience onto the meditation — for instance, confusing the joyful, unconditional cherishing in the mother meditation with the painful sense of dutiful obligation — and then wonder why it doesn't feel virtuous or inspired. Clarifying what the actual joyful, peaceful experience of the meditation is supposed to be can dissolve this completely.

Second: identify personal obstacles. Pride around independence, unresolved experiences of harm, misunderstandings about what the teaching is actually asking — these all create distortions. Third: ask why this meditation is specifically drawn out in the Lamrim at this point, what inner problems it solves that nothing else can. When we understand that, we become genuinely motivated. For instance, it was only when facing the full grip of craving that the contemplation on the faults of attachment suddenly became the most important meditation in the world — because it was the only medicine for a very real problem.

commentary.title: The Stepping-Stone Approach
content: Crossing a river in thick fog, you can only see the stone directly in front of you. You step onto it — and then the next stone becomes visible. And only then. From the shore, the third or fourth stone is completely invisible; it's not just difficult to see, it doesn't appear at all. A lot of Buddhist experience is like this: the understanding is experience-dependent, and each insight only becomes available once the previous one has been stabilized.

For us as practitioners and teachers, this means something practical. Bodhichitta is one of the stones in the river — but it only becomes real when great compassion is stable, which only becomes real when renunciation is powerful. We can talk about how beautiful it is on the far bank. But what actually moves people is being guided, stone by stone, to the next step that is genuinely available to them right now. The best class might simply be helping people clearly identify and step onto stone number one.

commentary.title: Getting the Terrain of Your Daily Life
content: One of the most important things we can do as practitioners is close the gap between the elevated teachings we've received and the actual texture of our lived life. The Dharma can easily stay abstract and generalized if we never apply it to the specific delusions we actually face on a Tuesday afternoon. The approach: think about one week at a time and ask, what is the terrain? What are the actual delusions that mess me up day to day? Then look for easy wins — places where a small intervention can make a real difference.

Like a humanitarian aid worker doing reconnaissance before entering a difficult area, we want a clear, honest sense of what we're actually working with. Not the grand aspirations, but the real ground. Minor non-acceptance, little craving moments, a quick flash of irritation — these are not too small. If we could completely unravel all of our minor non-acceptances in a single week, it would actually be a blissful week. That's where the magic really happens.
